1:
Whose word this is comes first. Gill says it was not the prophet’s own word but the Lord’s, taken up as a heavy burden, and insists it was to be heard though against them, since every word of God is to be hearkened to whether for us or against us. Henry presses the point: where God has a mouth to speak we must have an ear to hear, yet so stupid are most men that they need calling on again and again; the convincing word must be heeded as well as the words of comfort, for whether we hear or forbear it shall take effect and not a tittle fall to the ground. It is the word which I take up, he adds, not the prophet only but the God who sent him. Calvin adds that the Israelites did not think the punishment near and despised the denunciation, so that the prophet reproves indirectly the supine indifference in which they indulged.

Keil and Delitzsch give the plan of the whole. The elegy raised here forms the theme of the addresses that follow, divided into four parts by the admonitions to seek Jehovah and live, to seek good, and by the two woes; these have no purpose but to impress on the people the impossibility of averting the threatened destruction and to take from self-secure sinners the false foundations of their trust. In every section, they observe, the proclamation of judgment returns more intensely, until it reaches the banishment of the whole nation and the overthrow of Samaria and the kingdom.

Why Israel is called a virgin is the first real dispute. Gill offers three reasons: that the kingdom had never been subdued, that in its ecclesiastic state it had been espoused to the Lord as a chaste virgin, or that it is named from its wealth and splendour. Wesley takes the second without qualification, that so she was when first espoused to God. Calvin rejects that reading as too refined: expounders think the people so called because God had espoused them and they owed him spiritual chastity, but a virgin is a title the prophets give for the most part to a people on account of their delicacies, since Babylon no less than Samaria is called a virgin, and the refined reading cannot be applied to Babylon or Egypt or Tyre. He has no doubt the prophet arraigns the Israelites for relying on their strength and indulging themselves, quiet in their own retreats and living daintily. Ellicott takes a middle position, calling virgin a feminine designation poetically expressive of grace and beauty, like the epithet daughter of Zion, nations and cities being commonly personified as women. Henry keeps the beauty and drops the chastity: the state was not pure and chaste as a virgin, yet it was beautiful and gay and had its charms, and she was courted by many until she fell into contempt and was universally slighted.

How final the fall is divides them again. Clarke says the ten tribes were carried into captivity and are now totally lost in the nations of the earth. Ellicott qualifies it, that she is not annihilated but obliterated as a nation, and prefers to render the next word not forsaken but dashed to the earth; Wesley has her broken to pieces on her own land like a broken vessel. Calvin holds both halves together: the fall was not such that all were destroyed, since a tenth part would remain, yet it is rightly said of the people generally, for the kingdom so fell that it never rose again. He adds that a condition may be understood in the words, except they timely repent, since an exhortation to repentance immediately follows. Henry says flatly that she shall no more rise, God having begun to cut Israel short and, when they repented not, soon cutting Israel down.
3:
The arithmetic is plain. Clarke says the city that could easily have furnished a thousand fighting men can now produce scarcely a hundred, and of that hundred scarcely ten remain, so reduced was Israel when Samaria was taken and the residue carried into captivity. Ellicott puts it as a remnant of the thousand who went to war, the great cities being decimated in the coming struggle with Assyria; Wesley says the city that sent out a thousand shall lose nine parts of them; Gill takes the verse as the reason why none was left to raise the fallen up. Calvin turns the figure round. Armies were formerly decimated when a sedition had been made, but God threatens the Israelites here with a much heavier judgment, that only the tenth part would be saved from ruin rather than the tenth part lost.

Calvin explains why so small a mercy is mentioned at all. The prophet says more clearly what he had said before, that the kingdom would perish and yet the Lord preserve some remnants: as to the body of the people Israel had fallen, but a few were saved. Their wickedness was past hope, so the sentence of final ruin had to be announced; but it was so done as not to drive to despair the faithful few hid among the multitude. The word could not alleviate the grief of the people at large, and the hypocrites were the more exasperated at hearing that few would be saved, so that envy increased their griefs and embittered their minds; and that, Calvin says, was what the prophet designed, since it was of no use to apply solace to the despisers of God. But because God knew there was some seed remaining, he intended to provide for the miserable, who would otherwise have been swallowed up with grief.

The call to seek God is read by the others as an open offer. Gill takes the word that opens it as a yet: though the desolations would certainly come in case of impenitence and obstinate continuance in sin, hopes are given of finding mercy upon repentance, at least to the remnant. Clarke states it as a plea: cease your rebellion and return with all your heart, since though consigned to death ye shall be rescued and live, the case being deplorable but not utterly desperate. Ellicott takes the promise at its widest: search after God is rewarded by finding him, and this is life in the highest sense.

Calvin agrees the exhortation was common to all, then divides the calling in two. It was an address to everyone, though the greater part were past recovery, and necessary so long as they continued a chosen people, not yet abdicated; but the prophets preached to invite some to God and to render others inexcusable. With regard to the design of public teaching, he says, all are called in common; but God’s purpose is different, for he intends by his secret counsel to draw the elect to himself and to take away all excuse from the reprobate, that their obstinacy may be more apparent. Calvin adds a rule about the order of the clauses. The prophet first exhorts them to return to a sane mind and then offers the mercy of God if only they sought from the heart to be reconciled; and men cannot be led to repentance unless they believe God will be propitious to them, since all who think him implacable flee from him and dread the mention of his name. Were anyone to proclaim repentance through his whole life, he could effect nothing unless he connected the doctrine of faith with it. Henry reads the message the same way, as one in which they are told of their faults so that they might see what occasion there was to repent, and might not need to ask wherein they should return.
5:
The two shrines are named without ceremony. Gill says they must not go to Bethel, where one of the calves of Jeroboam was set up, to consult the oracle and the priests there; Wesley says the same in a line, that they must not consult or worship the idol at Bethel or Gilgal or Beersheba; Clarke adds that Gilgal too had its carved images, so that idolatry was triumphant in both places and all hope from those quarters is vain. Both Clarke and Ellicott hear a play upon words in the threat. Clarke renders it out: this Gilgal shall go captive into captivity, and Bethel, the house of God, shall be for Beth-aven, the house of iniquity. Ellicott says the play on Gilgal cannot be expressed accurately in translation, but follows an older rendering for the second name, that Bethel, the house of God, shall become Bethaven, the house of vanity, a form supported by the Greek version. He observes also that the verb rendered seek is the same word used for inquiring at idol shrines, which is what the prophet condemns.

Calvin makes the contrast between the two seekings the whole point of the verse. Some think the prophet is only repudiating the disguises hypocrites pretend, since when God calls such men they take indirect and tortuous courses; they see that they are justly reproved for departing from God, but when called back they go by a circuitous route, and though they pretend to seek him they are seeking subterfuges that they may not present themselves to him. All this is true, Calvin says, but the prophet advances further, showing that by going to Bethel the Israelites not only lost all their labour but grievously offended God, since superstition is in itself condemnable. Here he ascends higher and makes the two things wholly contrary, to seek God and to seek Bethel, as though he said, if ye return to me from the heart, renounce all the superstitions you have been attached to. It is a proof of true conversion, he adds, when the sinner is displeased with himself for his sins and hates the things that once pleased him, and with a changed mind devotes himself wholly to God.

Why the call is repeated is answered two ways. Gill says it is repeated to stir them up, because of their backwardness and slothfulness, and to show its importance and necessity. Calvin makes the repetition serve against the hearers rather than for them. It confirms that the opposition between true worship and superstition was such that the people, so long as they retained their corruptions, proved they had nothing to do with God whatever they pretended with mouth and ceremony; and the second call was useful so that hypocrites might know they were justly condemned. They were ever ready to contend with God, asking why he deals so strictly and concedes them nothing, since they do not deny him everything, and why he will not indulge them in what they think right; and when he visits them with punishments as well as words, they grow angry and raise a clamour. The prophet therefore calls a second time, as though to say that they will gain nothing by evasion, since whoever seeks God truly and from the heart will not be disappointed but received into favour and blessed; and if they pine away in their calamities they must impute it to their own obstinacy.

On the fire in the house of Joseph the notes are brief. Clarke identifies the house of Joseph as the Israelites of the ten tribes, of whom Ephraim and Manasseh were the chief. Ellicott would render the clause as a rushing down of fire upon the Northern Kingdom, and would read for Bethel rather than in Bethel; and he asks that the blending of mercy with judgment be observed, the curse being still conditional.
7:
The wormwood charge is aimed at the bench. Gill says it is spoken to kings and judges, in whose hands the administration of justice lies, so that what was most useful to the commonwealth is turned into something as bitter as wormwood, or hemlock as the word might be rendered. Ellicott sets the two words against each other, the holy thing judgment perverted into the bitter thing that is execrated, and would render the next clause as casting righteousness down to the earth by false judgments and unjust decrees; he reports a critic who moves this verse after the ninth, the two standing without any connecting link. Calvin sees the turn of the passage here: after inveighing against superstitions the prophet comes to the second table of the law, condemning two things expressly, that they had corrupted the worship of God and that they had acted dishonestly towards men, with plunder and cruelty and fraud.

Whether the doxology explains what precedes is disputed. Calvin says those who connect the verses and think the one explains the other are greatly mistaken, since they take God to be called righteousness by a metaphor and religion to be called judgment. He takes the verse by itself and answers that hypocrites trifle with God as though they had to do with a child, imagining a god after their own fancy and thinking him delighted with frivolous trifles, so that some little expiation is always ready; since they imagine God similar to a dead idol, the prophet shows that his nature is far otherwise. Ellicott has a grammatical version of the same problem, preferring to render the verse as concerning him who made the Pleiades rather than as a solemn assertion that there is one who maketh them; the effect, he says, is profoundly impressive amid the nature-worship of the East.

The constellations are glossed by three, and the seasons disagree. Clarke names them as the Hyades and Arcturus and reads the rest plainly, that God makes day and night, raises the waters of the sea by evaporation into clouds and pours them out in showers on the earth. Ellicott says the word for the seven stars means properly a heap or cluster and the word for Orion a stout or strong one, and that the appearance of the first marked the sweet influences of spring and the second the winter solstice; he notes that both this herdsman and Job, accustomed to the naked sky of the desert, make such references to astronomical facts, and finds in the death-shadow the darkest experiences of human life, on which God pours his light. Wesley dates the same risings differently, the seven stars rising about September with sweet showers and Orion about November with cold and rains and frosts intermixed.

The last line reads two ways. Gill, Clarke and Wesley take it as a reversal in favour of the weak: the spoiled, stripped of armour and goods, are supplied with strength and sent helpers, so that they rise against their conquerors, God taking the part of the oppressed and setting up the one while he depresses the other, until the besieged rally and besiege their besiegers. Ellicott renders it otherwise, that God causes desolation to gleam upon the strong, who were priding themselves on their immunity, so that desolation comes upon the stronghold. Calvin is nearer to Ellicott in effect: God will stir up robbers who will beat in pieces the obduracy by which the Israelites now resist him, and their confidence in fortified cities and a powerful army will be useless when he raises up depredators who penetrate well-fortified gates and leap over walls. Henry draws the moral: the same almighty power can turn the affliction of repenting sinners into prosperity and the prosperity of daring sinners into darkness, and whereas the judgments of God had often passed by sinful Israel, now they shall pass through them.
10:
Who hates the reprover, and who the reprover is, are both open. Gill offers two readings and chooses: either wicked judges hated the prophets who reproved them for perverting justice even while they sat on the bench, or the people were so degenerate that they hated the faithful judges who reproved their vices in open court; the former seems to him best. Wesley leaves both in, saying the haters are the judges and the people, and adds that the gate was where judges sat and where the prophets many times delivered their message. Ellicott suggests that the reprover so described might be the prophet himself, and likewise the one who speaks uprightly. Clarke gives the charge in a line, that they cannot bear an upright magistrate and will not have righteous laws executed.

Calvin agrees the judges are meant, though the words might extend to the whole people, since nearly the whole discourse is levelled against the judges. When they sat in the gate and perverted justice, and any man reminded them of their duty, they haughtily rejected all admonitions and hated those who gave them: they who ought to correct whatever vice there is among the people cannot themselves bear a reprover when their own vices require strong remedies. Calvin then says the disease is not of one age only. Kings and those in authority wish to be deemed sacred and will allow no reproof, so that the majesty of God is thought to be violated in their persons, and they cry out whenever servants of God dare to lay open their wicked conduct; even now those who occupy the seats of judgment would claim a free liberty in sinning, not thinking themselves of the common class of men.

The oppression is described in the same terms by everyone and priced differently. Gill takes the verse as spoken to princes and magistrates who oppressed the poor and crushed them to the ground, stripping them of the little they had and exercising a tyrannical power over men who had none to stand by them. Clarke sharpens the figure, that the poor are trodden under foot and form the road on which their oppressors walk, and yet it was by impoverishing them that those riches were gained. Wesley says simply that they utterly oppress the helpless and extort from the poor great quantities of the wheat on which he should live. Calvin makes the same point about the target: the prophet contends not with the common people but attacks the chief men, since from them proceeded all the prevailing evil, and he doubts not the judges are accused of burdening miserable men with tributes and exactions.

On the burdens of wheat the readings differ in what exactly is taken. Clarke makes it a fee for justice, that they will have the poor man’s bread for doing him right. Ellicott makes it a gift rather than a fee: they take sifted corn as a contribution to their own luxury, which the poor man was not bound to offer and would offer only to purchase their good will; and therefore, he says, their pomp and luxury shall be of no avail, such being the judgment of God on indifference to the wants and the feelings of the poor. Calvin notes a difficulty in the word for treading. It may be taken as a burden laid on the poor or as a trampling of them, and it matters little which; he remarks that it is not often one meets a verb of four letters, and that in a number of manuscripts one letter is left out. Keil and Delitzsch add a small rule about the therefore that opens the sentence, that this word always introduces the threatening of divine punishment after the exposure of the sins.
12:
Who says that he knows is the first question. Calvin has God introduced as the speaker so that the threatening might be more authoritative, since the prophets were despised by haughty men, but when God himself appeared before them it was strange if no fear laid hold on them. Since the rich covered every wickedness by their splendour, and the magistrates most of all, God tells them their turpitude was fully known to him, so that they would gain nothing by subtle evasions. Ellicott dissents. Most commentators imply that the speaker is Jehovah, but he thinks it more likely the prophet himself; and he would render the adjectives as predicates, that manifold are your transgressions and mighty your sins, ye afflicters of the just and takers of a bribe.

What the sins were is listed plainly. Clarke says the multitude of their smaller crimes has been marked as well as their mighty offences, and names three among the greater, afflicting the righteous, taking bribes to blind their eyes in judgment, and refusing to hear the poor who had no money to give them. Ellicott sharpens the second: the word rendered bribe carries the idea of a ransom which the poor and defenceless were obliged to pay a tyrannical judge to escape a harsh sentence, the gate being where judgment is passed by the chief men. Calvin adds a distinction about degree: when something is done amiss by the highest power indulgence is commonly granted, since nothing is harder than for one who sustains so great a burden to remain free from every blame; but the Lord shows they were not lightly culpable, their crimes being too grievous to be endured.

Who the prudent are that keep silence divides them most sharply. Gill excludes the prophets: it was their business at all times to reprove, whatever the consequence, though the Targum calls the silent ones teachers. He takes them for private persons, whose wisdom it would be to say nothing, since reproof would do no good and would bring hatred and trouble upon themselves. Calvin canvasses the opposite. One exposition, which he thinks probable, is that the prudent dared not speak on account of the prevailing tyranny, since the judges would not bear reproof, so that every liberty of teaching was taken away; the silent had to bear their wrongs and devour their own groans, and the very teachers did not oppose the torrent, seeing it was not the time to resist violent men.

Calvin sets one reading aside and leaves two standing. Some interpreters, he says, think a punishment is here denounced, that the Lord would deprive the people of prophets and teachers; and though nothing is more to be dreaded than that God should extinguish the light of sound doctrine, he rejects that exposition as having nothing in its favour. The verse may also be applied to the judgment of God another way, that the prudent would be silent from fear, and it is a dreadful judgment of God when the prudent closes his mouth or lays his hand upon it. Why the silence is prudent the others answer differently. Clarke makes it a calculation: a wise man will consider that it is useless to complain, since he can have no justice without bribes and has no money to give, so that in such an evil time it is best to say nothing. Wesley says the silence is forced, and calls the time evil both for the sinfulness of it and for the troubles and wars and captivity now at hand. Ellicott makes the silence itself the sentence, the dumb silence of the prudent being the awful curse that comes upon a people given up to selfishness and rapacity. Gill offers one more sense, that they would not speak to God on behalf of these men, knowing the decree was gone forth, nor murmur against it, believing it righteous.
14:
Calvin reads the renewed call as a defence of God against the people’s complaints. It was owing to the Israelites themselves that it was not well with them, since God was ready to grant his blessing while they designedly sought a curse. Hypocrites put the blame of every evil away from themselves and complain as though the Lord afflicted them unjustly; so the prophet shows that no evil happened to them but what they procured by their own vices, while exhorting them to repentance and giving hope of pardon if they do not harden their hearts to the last. The added words, and not evil, Calvin finds full of meaning, as though they were so fixed in their wickedness that they could not be torn from it, being not merely alienated from good but following evil with avidity.

Clarke states the same thing as a puzzle: is there a greater mystery in the world than that a man, instead of seeking good, will seek evil, knowing that it is evil? And since God is the fountain of good, they who seek the supreme good seek him, and they who seek shall find him. Gill expands the object of the search, taking the good to be first God himself, the chief good, the fountain of all goodness and the portion of his people; then Christ, the good Saviour and the good Shepherd; and then the good Spirit, who works good things in his people and is their comforter.

On the clause about what they say, Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin meet. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the command to seek and love good is practically the same as the earlier command to seek the Lord, and carries the same promise; but it is only in fellowship with God that a man has life, and this truth the Israelites had laid hold of in a perfectly outward sense, fancying they stood in that fellowship as sons of Israel or of Abraham, so that the threatened judgment could not reach them and God would deliver them in every time of oppression. Calvin reproves the same wickedness in a people who sought to bind God to themselves: hypocrites misapply the promises, and while they presumptuously reject God himself they still wish him under obligation to them, glorying in being the children of Abraham, circumcision being to them like a royal diadem.

Why hating comes before loving is Calvin’s point in the next verse. The prophet inculcates the same truth designedly, since nothing was harder than to bring this people to repentance, refractory by nature and hardened by long habit; for Satan gains dominion by degrees until he renders men wholly stupid, so that they no longer discern between right and wrong, and such was the blindness in Israel that it was necessary to goad them often. The order ought to be kept: he begins with hating evil because he addresses men so immersed in wickedness that they no longer distinguished light from darkness, and because, while such an exhortation is superfluous for one already wishing to devote himself to God, a man still sunk in his vices needs the stimulant. Gill puts the two halves in parallel: evil is to be hated for its own nature and pernicious consequences and, if for no other reason, because it is hateful to God, and good is to be loved for goodness sake. Clarke reduces it to a rule: what ruins you is to be avoided and what helps you cleaved to, the proof of taking the advice being to purify the seats of justice. On the remnant of Joseph, Clarke understands the posterity of the ten tribes, while Wesley limits it to what the invasions of enemies and the civil wars had left in Samaria and Israel; and Wesley reads the command to love good as a charge to commend and encourage and defend it.
16:
What the therefore looks back to gets two answers. Gill says the connection is not with the preceding words but with the whole context, since neither promises nor threats nor exhortations had any effect on the generality of the people. Calvin takes the particle of inference as confirming that the Israelites vainly flattered themselves though they were in the worst condition; and since there would be no end to the evasions of such perverse hypocrites, the prophet cuts them off by declaring that God has announced his purpose, so that his judgment can no longer be deferred, their iniquity being sufficiently proved.

The piling up of the divine names is remarked on. Henry says the threatening is introduced with more than ordinary solemnity, to strike an awe upon them: it is not the word of the prophet only, which might be made light of, but of the Lord Jehovah who has an infinite eternal being, of the God of hosts who has boundless irresistible power, and of Adonai who has an absolute sovereignty and a universal dominion. Ellicott adds that the title Lord of hosts marks the antithesis between the Portion of Jacob and all the deities of the heathen.

The mourning is described street by street. Henry has the lamentation so great that it is not confined within doors nor kept within the bounds of decency, but proclaimed in the streets and highways and running wild, with wailing in the great streets and the by-streets and the cry that they are all undone along the country roads. Ellicott corrects the geography, the streets being the open squares near the gates and the highways more properly the narrow alleys of the crowded cities of the East, and notes that the word for wailing denotes properly the beating of the breast. Those skilled in wailing, he adds, were generally women who tear their hair and dress and throw dust over the head and utter the monotonous wail of distress; and he would invert the last clause, so that wailing is called to such as are skilful of lamentation. Henry makes the same distinction in his own terms: the husbandman is called from the plough to the natural expressions of mourning, and because those come short of the merits of the cause, the skilful mourners are called in to the artificial kind.

Why the husbandman is called is answered differently. Clarke gives an agricultural reason: the crops have failed and the ground has been tilled in vain. Ellicott and Wesley make it a measure of extent: the calling of the husbandman away indicates that the disaster was universal, and this sort of men, Wesley says, are little used to such ceremonies, yet now they too must leave their toil for public mourning. In the vineyards the point is made by contrast, Gill observing that where there used to be great shoutings and joy at the vintage there shall now be a different tone, and Clarke and Wesley agreeing that these were the places where festivity especially prevailed.

The passing through is the sharpest word here. Calvin observes that nothing was more to be desired than that God should visit his own land, and that he here declares he will pass through it as an enemy, spreading devastation wherever he comes. He takes the prophet to allude to the passing of God through Egypt described by Moses, when no corner was safe from his wrath, so that Israel would now be as Egypt was, and he who once testified his love toward the children of Abraham would show himself their enemy. Clarke makes the same allusion briefly, that God will pass through as he passed through Egypt by the destroying angel, not to spare but to destroy; Wesley says simply that it is to punish all everywhere. Ellicott generalises: wherever Jehovah passes through a land or city, heavy punishment is intended.
18:
Who desires the day of the Lord, and why, is answered several ways. Gill offers two: either the coming of Christ in the flesh, desired not for spiritual salvation but for deliverance from outward troubles, or else the day of judgment they had been threatened with, which they did not believe would come, so that they asked for it scoffingly to show they were in no fear about it. Clarke and Wesley take the second only, Clarke recalling that the unbelievers had said, let his day come that we may see it. Henry supplies a third sort, those who wish for times of war and confusion in hope of rising upon their country’s ruins, and answers that the desolation would be so great that nobody could gain by it. Ellicott states the reversal in a figure: they expect deliverance and judgment on their enemies, and it shall bring the reverse, for there is a dark side to the pillar of fire.

Calvin takes the woe as aimed at a particular temper. The Israelites acted strangely in setting up the name of God as their shield and entertaining hope though oppressed with many evils, because God had promised they should be objects of his care; this was an extremely vain pretence. The Spirit everywhere treats hypocrites with more severity than the openly impious, since the despisers of God do not excuse their vices, while hypocrites seek to draw God into the quarrel and have veils to cover their turpitude. He also rejects a reading: some expound the day of Jehovah of the day of death and think the prophet speaks of desperate men who seek self-destruction by hanging or poison, but the prophet is rousing hypocrites, not describing suicides.

The chain of escapes is read alike, illustrated differently. Gill has the man flee at the sight of a lion only to be met by a bear, a less generous and more cruel creature, especially when bereaved of its whelps; Ellicott says the escape will be impossible; Wesley notes that at home a man may hope for safety and there another kind of mischief meets him. Clarke supplies a historical instance: the Israelites under Menahem, to avoid a civil war, called in the king of Assyria, which led to a series of evils until Israel was ravaged by Shalmaneser and carried into captivity, so that in avoiding one evil they fell into a worse.

Calvin uses it to separate two kinds of hope. Hypocrites promise better things to themselves when the times change, and as Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, so they imitate the true servants of God; but it is a false imitation, fading flowers with no fruit following, not proceeding from a living root. The faithful, when they promise themselves a prosperous issue, are touched at the same time with a sense of their own evils and study to be reconciled to God, whereas hypocrites remain immersed in their vices and boldly despise him.

The repeated question is taken as emphasis. Gill says its design is to affirm that in this day there should be nothing but misery and distress; Ellicott says the word rendered very dark is the one used of the gross Egyptian darkness that might be felt, a gloom accompanied by confusion and terror and intolerable suspense. Calvin adds that the Lord will not come except armed, and will bring no light except to fulminate, so that when he ceases to pursue them one way he will assail them another, and when foreign enemies spare them he will destroy them at home by sterility or pestilence. Yet the prophet did not intend to drive all into despair, but to shake self-flattery off hypocrites: put off the perverse conduct and God would be ready to pardon. Henry ends on the same note: when God makes a day dark, all the world cannot make it light.
21:
Whose feasts are meant comes first. Gill reports that Kimchi refers the words to the kingdom of Judah, which kept the feasts the Lord had commanded, but thinks it not necessary to understand them so, since the ten tribes doubtless imitated the worship at Jerusalem and trusted in the observance of them; the Lord rejects that vain confidence and lets them know the feasts were in no way acceptable, so far from atoning for their sins that they were hated and despised. Henry fills the imitation out: they had their feast-days at Bethel after the pattern of those at Jerusalem, and their solemn assemblies, in which they put on the gravity of those who come before God as his people come and sit before him as his people sit; they offered burnt-offerings to his honour with the meat-offerings belonging to them, and peace-offerings of their fat beasts to implore his favour, and in imitation of the temple-music they had the noise of their songs and the melody of their viols. Clarke says the words may refer to the three annual festivals still observed in a certain way among them, and that God abominates sacrificial festivals where there is no piety and despises them because they pretend to be what they are not.

Why the worship is hateful and not merely useless Henry puts strongly. With these services they hoped to make God amends for the sins they had committed and to obtain leave to go on in sin, and so they were not merely unacceptable but abominable: he hated their feast-days as an affront and a provocation, as we hate to see men dissemble with us and pretend a respect they do not have. Nothing, Henry says, is more hateful than hypocrisy, and he that blesseth his friend with a loud voice shall have it counted a curse when his heart is not with him.

Calvin agrees the sacrifices are rejected, then separates his prophet from the common complaint. Sacrifices are often reprehended by the prophets when not accompanied by godliness and sincerity, since God commanded them only as religious exercises, which had to be joined with penitence and faith; hypocrites thought that by them they discharged their whole duty, which was itself a profanation, and though the Jews had not departed from the law as to external form, their sacrifices were vicious, impurity of heart vitiating all their works. But the design of this prophet, Calvin thinks, was different: he blamed the Israelites not only because they falsely pretended the name of God in their sacrifices, but because they were apostates who had departed from the teaching of the law and built for themselves a spurious temple. Gill lists the defects in order: the offerings were made neither in a proper place nor in a right manner according to the law, nor in the faith of the great sacrifice, nor with repentance.

On the words themselves the notes are small. Calvin observes that the term rendered meat offering properly means a gift of flour added to a sacrifice, though often taken for any kind of offering, and that however much the Israelites accumulated their observances they did nothing towards appeasing God, since they spread veils before him, hoping by a fictitious worship to cover their sins and thinking themselves hidden. He notes too that the prophet alludes to the promises of the law, where Moses often says God is delighted with the odour of sacrifices; but the Lord means that odour pleasant only if the people sacrificed rightly, bringing their offerings not as veils to cover sin but as true evidences of faith and repentance. Clarke adds a lexical guess, that the word for the fat beasts probably means buffaloes. Keil and Delitzsch state the upshot: this heartless worship would not arrest the flood of divine judgments, since Israel had from time immemorial been addicted to idolatry.
23:
The music is dismissed sharply, and each finds his own reason. Gill says the ten tribes very probably imitated the temple music at Jerusalem, vocal and instrumental, but that their music is called a noise, being disagreeable to the Lord as coming from such carnal and wicked persons. Clarke divides the two halves: God hated the noise of the one and shut his ears against the melody of the other, since in the first there was nothing but noise, their hearts not being right with God, and in the second nothing but cutting and scraping, there being no religious sense in the thing nor in those who used it. Ellicott says the very sound of their tumultuous songs was a burden to Jehovah, and that as Christ cleansed the Temple so would he dispel this hypocritical confusion of ideas. Wesley notes only that the songs were used in their sacrifices and solemn feasts in imitation of the temple worship, that not hearing means not hearing with acceptance, and that the one instrument named stands for all the rest.

Calvin fastens on the word multitude. By speaking of a multitude of songs the prophet aims at hypocrites, who toil in their devices without measure or end, accumulating endless forms of worship and wearying themselves morning and evening, every one devising some new thing and all heaped together. When men have once begun to turn aside from the pure word of God they continually invent trifles, and the prophet touches indirectly on this foolish laboriousness; he might simply have said, thy songs please me not, but he mentions their multitude, because hypocrites fix no limits to their ceremonies once they take the liberty of devising this or that form of worship. Calvin adds two smaller notes, that the instrument named is of a kind now unknown, and that it seems most probable to join the two clauses together, taking away the multitude of songs and the harmony of lyres with which the singer thinks God delighted, and to take the refusal to hear by itself.

The command that follows is read by most as exhortation. Gill takes the verb as rolling, and hears in it abundance and rapidity, justice bearing down all before it so that nothing can resist, which signifies the plenty of justice done in the land and the full and free exercise of it. Wesley reduces it to a rule: justice administered constantly, righteousness meaning equity, the stream bearing down all that opposes it. Clarke draws the two figures apart: let the execution of justice be everywhere like the showers that fall upon the land to render it fertile, and righteousness in heart and life like a mighty river, or like the Jordan, that winds through the whole nation and carries every abomination into the Dead Sea. Ellicott offers one word, that the mighty stream is rather a perennial one.

Calvin surveys three expositions and settles on the middle. To some the verse seems an exhortation, as though the prophet said that they thrust on him victims and ceremonies while he regards none of them, since interior purity of heart alone pleases him, so that they should bring what he especially requires. Some think newness of life is described here by its fruits, since the prophet mentions neither purity nor faith nor repentance but sets forth by the fruits that renovation which God chiefly regards; on this view hypocrites are recalled to true worship, and by requiring righteousness and judgment the prophet requires a holy and pure life. Others think he turns aside to celebrate the grace of Christ made known in the gospel, the verb being rendered by many as shall be revealed, though others more correctly derive it from a root meaning to roll; on that reading the gospel is compared to an impetuous river, because the Lord would rush on and penetrate all hindrances.
25:
The question about the forty years is the hardest here. Gill answers flatly in the negative: the sacrifices were offered not to God but to devils, to the golden calf and to the host of heaven; and Wesley asks the same, whether it was to God or to their idols that they offered even in the wilderness. Clarke will not have the question mean that no sacrifices at all were offered. Some have thought the Israelites sacrificed nothing during those years, but that forgets the burnt-offerings at the making of the covenant and the offerings of the twelve princes at the setting up of the tabernacle, which came to an immense number over twelve days, besides the bullocks and rams at the consecration of the priests. They were not offered so regularly nor in such abundance as after the settlement, and so learned men take the question to be whether they offered in a way pleasing to God, and answer that they did not.

Calvin uses the verse to show that the disease was not new. The prophet is not only reproving hypocrisy in obtruding ceremonies without religion of heart, but condemning a departure from the rule of the law, since at the very beginning the fathers had mixed a leaven that vitiated the worship of God. He addresses men born many ages later as though they had themselves perverted worship in the desert, enclosing them in the same bundle with their fathers, since they were the same in their ways and dispositions.

What they carried is disputed, and so is the tense. Keil and Delitzsch take the verse adversatively, that to Jehovah they offered no sacrifices but they bore these other things, and hold the opposition between the worship they suspended and the idolatry they carried on so clearly expressed by the two answering verbs that a rival view is untenable, which would make the words a threat that they shall carry the hut of their king into exile. The idea of idols carried into captivity is utterly foreign to the prophetic range of thought, since it is not those who go into captivity who carry their gods away, but the gods of a vanquished nation that are carried off by the conquerors. Clarke sets the two verses against each other another way, the earlier speaking of the fathers and this of the Israelites then living, who carried their gods about with them everywhere in a small portable shrine.

The names themselves are uncertain. Gill takes the first for the god of the Ammonites, but allows that the word may be the proper name of an idol, as several Jewish interpreters take it, given the title of king as another idol was called the queen of heaven, perhaps the one meaning the sun and the other the moon. Calvin makes a textual judgment about the same word: the place is quoted in the Acts from the Greek version, and the Greek translator was mistaken, reading it as a plural appellative from a term meaning a tabernacle, whereas it was probably the proper name of an idol.

Why Damascus is named at the end is a question Calvin says interpreters have not noticed. The Israelites thought all attacks of enemies were kept off by that city, which they supposed impregnable, and the sense is that the fortress will not prevent God from removing them as far as the Assyrians. On the difference between the prophet and the quotation in the Acts, which reads beyond Babylon, Calvin says the meaning and not the words is given, Clarke that the Spirit chose to extend the sense to the later captivity, and Gill that the way to Media lay through Syria and Babylon. Calvin ends on the closing title, finding it apt that men who had become worshippers of the hosts of heaven should be told that Jehovah is the God of hosts.
